name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 23 February 1973

blocks.note: the county town of Berkshire, a place in Berks
apartments are rooms, especially a set of them

explanation.surface: A note on student lodgings to be found in Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Berks is the abbreviation for Berkshire, an English county whose county town is Reading; apartments there are rooms in Reading, yet the whole phrase is also library rooms where students sit to study.
explanation.definitionFit: Libraries provide quiet halls where scholars sit to study, so these are places students occupy, punningly called apartments.

blocks.note: surface reading: a petty criminal who is not part of organised crime
setter's reading: a racket is also a loud noise, and this thief makes only a soft rustling sound, not a racket

explanation.surface: A small-time crook who has nothing to do with organised rackets.
explanation.walkthrough: Racketeer suggests gangland extortion, but a racket is also a din; the thief's name comes from a quiet sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler steals livestock, especially cattle or horses, so is a particular kind of thief.

blocks.note: first meaning: amounts of surface, measured in square units
second meaning: sunken paved yards in front of a basement, below street level

explanation.surface: A query about how the minor law courts are measured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tho' is a misprint for 'the'. Lower courts look legal, but they are the sunken yards outside British basement flats, called areas.
explanation.definitionFit: Square-footage figures are measurements of space, and the British basement courtyard is traditionally called the area.

clue.text: I will go; nett rise is dis honestly obtained

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read from the bottom upward, so backwards

blocks.note: contraction I'll, without its apostrophe
taken as written
taken as written, then turned round

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to leave, while net profits are said to come from shady dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dis honestly' is the printed form of dishonestly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-gotten gains are money acquired by fraud or other improper means, never earned fairly.

indicators.note: sounds says we want a word heard as a spoken form, spelt differently

blocks.note: a Gael is a Celtic Scot or Irish person; the girl's name is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: A woman whose voice has a Scottish or Irish lilt.
explanation.walkthrough: A single pronoun can define a female first name in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Gail is a woman's first name, so a female person can be referred to by the pronoun given.

blocks.note: overt means done openly, not hidden
an urn is a vase-shaped vessel

explanation.surface: An uncovered vase is easy to knock over and spill.
explanation.definitionFit: To spill a vessel is to tip it over, upsetting the contents, which is to overturn it.

blocks.note: surface reading: a young woman giving shelter to lawbreakers
setter's reading: the girl's name that follows Black in the slang name of a police van that carries arrested people

explanation.surface: A young woman who shelters lawbreakers.
explanation.walkthrough: A Black Maria is the old slang term for a police van used to carry prisoners.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria is a common woman's first name, and also the second word of the police van's nickname.

definitions.note: a description of the answer, which is a plural noun: things got cheaply

blocks.note: a bar is a pub or a drinking room in one
gains are profits

explanation.surface: A publican's takings come easily.
explanation.definitionFit: Bargains are items purchased below their usual price, acquired for little money.

clue.text: Signal to stop horseplay maddens certain speculators

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: the thing that maddens them

blocks.note: a red light or flag means stop
a rag is a boisterous prank or student horseplay

explanation.surface: A warning to end rowdy behaviour, which upsets some investors.
explanation.walkthrough: Bulls are stock-market speculators who expect rising prices; a red rag to a bull is the proverbial thing that enrages.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving a scarlet cloth is said to enrage a bull, and certain stock investors are known as bulls.

clue.text: Bombardment goes South to Dashwood's Club

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation
Sir Francis Dashwood founded the notorious eighteenth-century Hellfire Club

explanation.surface: A shelling campaign heads south toward a gentleman's club.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hellfire Club was a scandalous society of rakes founded by Sir Francis Dashwood in 1700s England.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellfire is artillery fire of exploding projectiles, the substance of any bombardment by big guns.

clue.text: It is never too late to mend Charles

blocks.clueFragment: It is never too late to mend Charles
blocks.note: surface reading: an encouragement that a man named Charles can still reform

blocks.clueFragment: It is never too late to mend
blocks.note: setter's reading: the title of an 1856 novel, whose author was named Charles

explanation.surface: A reassurance that Charles can still change his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is also the title of a Victorian novel; the clue asks for its author's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was the Victorian novelist who wrote the book with that proverb as its title.

clue.text: Instruction one has in hot weather

definitions.note: a phrase describing what one has on: less clothing

blocks.note: first meaning: a period of teaching, a class
second meaning, split in two: in summer heat one wears fewer clothes

explanation.surface: Teaching that someone gets during a heatwave.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads as two words, LESS ON: what one has on when it is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson is a session of teaching, a unit of instruction given to pupils.

blocks.note: St is the address abbreviation
a Ranger was a senior member of the Girl Guides

explanation.surface: The person showing visitors round the street turns out to be from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A stranger is someone unknown or from another place, like an outsider from abroad.

clue.text: This will perhaps be rate of deduction

indicators.note: perhaps hints these letters might be something else, so they get rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark about what the rate of a tax deduction will be.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebate is a partial refund or reduction of a sum owed, so an amount knocked off.

blocks.note: the best is the finest
to horse, as a verb, is to ride

explanation.surface: A recommendation to get up on the best horse in the stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horse' looks like a noun but works as a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestride is to sit astride with legs on either side, as when getting on a horse.

blocks.note: the Cree are a Native American people
a ping is a short ringing sound

explanation.surface: A slow passage of music from India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'movement' suggests a section of a symphony, and 'Indian' the subcontinent; here it is a North American people.
explanation.definitionFit: Creeping is crawling forward stealthily, progress made at a gradual crawl.

blocks.note: the pupil is the dark centre of the eye, standing for the whole
to shine is to be bright

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy that makes a schoolchild glow.
explanation.walkthrough: The herb was traditionally used to treat sore eyes, which gives the clue its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphrasia is the botanical genus name for the small wild flower once used in eye lotions.

blocks.note: first meaning: an old sense, set at large, freed from prison
second meaning: made bigger

explanation.surface: Someone freed and given a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe is a misprint. The first sense is archaic, from being set at large.
explanation.definitionFit: Something made bigger has grown in size, and an old legal sense means released from custody.

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so these letters must be set right again

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor calls something from the back of the ship and is told it is incorrect.
explanation.definitionFit: A resonant sound is deep and reverberating, filling a space and ringing on like an echo.

blocks.note: rep is a ribbed fabric
to be on the air is to be broadcast on radio

explanation.surface: An instruction to mend some fabric, heard on a broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece 'on' another sits above it.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good damage is to fix it, restoring something to working order.

blocks.note: surface reading: the long Russian ambition for a warm-water sea outlet
setter's reading: a sea belonging to the communist state, whose colour is the one associated with communism

explanation.surface: Moscow's longstanding wish for a presence in warm southern waters.
explanation.walkthrough: Red was the colour of Soviet Russia, so a Russian sea would be a red one; the real sea links to the Mediterranean through Suez.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Sea is the narrow body of water between Africa and Arabia, joined by canal to the Mediterranean.

blocks.note: surface reading: ominous omens, or markers on tombs
setter's reading: grave is a type of mark over a letter, like é or è, one example of a wider class

explanation.surface: Perhaps these are ominous portents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' shows the grave mark is one example; acute and circumflex are others.
explanation.definitionFit: Accents are marks placed over letters to show pronunciation, and the grave is one kind.

clue.text: Apparent displacement when gunners hold everything in plea for peace

indicators.note: in places the first words inside the plea, which wraps round them

blocks.note: pax is Latin for peace, called out as a plea for a truce
RA is the Royal Artillery, the British army's gunners
all means everything

explanation.surface: Artillerymen holding everything up while asking for a ceasefire.
explanation.walkthrough: Pax was a British schoolchild's cry for a truce.
explanation.definitionFit: Parallax is the seeming shift in an object's position when viewed from two different points.

clue.text: Yarn that brings money to the island

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for pound sterling, from Latin libra
an isle is an island

explanation.surface: A tale about bringing cash to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' tempts as a story; here it is thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisle is a fine, strong cotton thread, used especially for stockings.

blocks.note: first meaning: a reviewer who assesses works of art
second meaning: the title of Sheridan's 1779 comic play

explanation.surface: Someone who assesses funny plays.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Brinsley Sheridan's play The Critic is a satirical comedy about theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer evaluates and passes verdict on books or performances, and Sheridan's farce bears that title.

blocks.note: taken as written
ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state

explanation.surface: The atmosphere of a New England state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'air' suggests breeze; here it is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is a main melody in a piece of music, and an air is likewise a tune.

indicators.note: anyhow means in any careless order, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: a misprint for live, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone named Jacobson might dance in any old style.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has misprints: it should read 'Jacob's son may live anyhow'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Levi was the third son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the priestly tribe.

clue.text: Try hard work on this river

indicators.note: on says the first word would sit on the end of the answer; we take it back off

blocks.note: industry means diligent effort
taken as written, the part removed

explanation.surface: An invitation to some strenuous labour on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Put TRY on the end of the river and you get INDUSTRY; so the river is INDUSTRY without TRY.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus is the great river flowing through Pakistan into the Arabian Sea.

definitions.note: a noun, while the answer is usually an adjective

blocks.note: Lady Jane Grey was the nine-days queen of England in 1553
green with envy means jealous

explanation.surface: A noblewoman envious of someone's complexion.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey-green is a muted shade of greenish grey, a hue or tint used in paint.

clue.text: Principal job of Casanova's best girl?

blocks.note: first meaning: the woman in charge of a school
second meaning, split in two: the chief of a famous seducer's lovers

explanation.surface: Wondering about the main role of a famous lover's favourite woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Casanova was an 18th-century Venetian famed for his many lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: A headmistress is the female head of a school, its principal; read in two parts it is a chief lover.
